questions.q: State the Law of Definite Proportions and the Law of Multiple Proportions in your own words.
questions.a: Law of Definite Proportions: A given compound always contains the same elements in the same fixed proportion by mass. Law of Multiple Proportions: When two elements form more than one compound, the masses of one element that combine with a fixed mass of the other are in a ratio of small whole numbers. A wrong answer (e.g., confusing the two laws or stating "fixed ratio by volume") reveals the student has not distinguished between mass-based and volume-based laws, or has memorized without understanding the "fixed mass of one element" condition in the second law.

questions.q: Why does the Law of Definite Proportions hold true for pure compounds but not for mixtures? Explain using the particle nature of matter.
questions.a: A pure compound consists of identical molecules (or formula units) with a fixed number of atoms of each element, so the mass ratio is constant. A mixture contains physically combined substances in variable proportions, so its overall composition can change. A wrong answer (e.g., "mixtures are impure") shows the student lacks the particulate understanding that compounds have fixed stoichiometry at the molecular level while mixtures do not.

questions.q: Two oxides of nitrogen are analyzed. Oxide A: 1.00 g contains 0.636 g N. Oxide B: 1.00 g contains 0.467 g N. Show that these data obey the Law of Multiple Proportions. (Atomic masses: N=14, O=16)
questions.a: For Oxide A: mass O = 0.364 g. Mass of O per 1 g N = 0.364/0.636 = 0.572 g. For Oxide B: mass O = 0.533 g. Mass of O per 1 g N = 0.533/0.467 = 1.141 g. Ratio of oxygen masses (B:A) = 1.141/0.572 = 1.995 ≈ 2:1. This simple whole-number ratio confirms the Law of Multiple Proportions. A wrong answer (e.g., comparing percentages directly without fixing nitrogen mass) reveals the student misses the critical step of "fixing the mass of one element" before comparing.

questions.q: A student analyzes two samples of water: one from the Ganga river and one from melted Himalayan ice. Both give 11.11% H and 88.89% O by mass. The student concludes this proves the Law of Definite Proportions. Is this conclusion valid? Justify.
questions.a: Yes, the conclusion is valid because the law states that a given compound (water) has the same elemental composition by mass regardless of source. The identical percentages from two different natural sources confirm the law. A wrong answer (e.g., "no, because natural water has impurities") shows the student confuses the purity of the sample with the law's application to the pure compound; the law applies to the compound itself, and the experiment assumes pure water samples.

questions.q: Evaluate the following statement: "The Law of Multiple Proportions is a direct consequence of the Law of Definite Proportions." True or false? Explain.
questions.a: False. The Law of Definite Proportions deals with the fixed composition of a single compound. The Law of Multiple Proportions compares the compositions of two or more different compounds formed from the same elements. The latter is not a logical consequence of the former; both are independent experimental laws that Dalton's atomic theory explains. A wrong answer (e.g., "true, because both deal with fixed ratios") reveals the student does not distinguish between intra-compound and inter-compound relationships.

questions.q: Design a simple experiment (using only a balance and common chemicals) to verify the Law of Definite Proportions for magnesium oxide. Outline the procedure, measurements, and calculation.
questions.a: Procedure: 1) Weigh a clean, dry crucible. 2) Add a known mass of magnesium ribbon (e.g., 0.50 g). 3) Heat strongly with lid slightly ajar until reaction completes (Mg + ½O₂ → MgO). 4) Cool and weigh the crucible + product. 5) Calculate mass of oxygen gained = (mass of product) - (mass of Mg). 6) Compute %Mg and %O. Repeat with a different mass of Mg (e.g., 0.80 g). If both trials give ~60.3% Mg and ~39.7% O, the law is verified. A poor answer (e.g., "mix Mg and O₂ gas in a jar") shows the student cannot design a controlled combustion experiment or account for oxygen mass by difference.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: The Law of Definite ______ states that a given chemical compound always contains its constituent elements in a fixed ratio by mass, regardless of its source or method of preparation.
Fill in the blank: Begin by showing the student two samples of copper(II) oxide: one prepared by heating copper in air (black powder) and another by ______ copper(II) nitrate (also black powder).
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can verify experimental data for compliance with the Law of Definite Proportions by calculating mass ratios, and can apply the Law of Multiple Proportions to determine the whole-number mass ratio between two compounds of the same elements.
